Claude and Codex framing: capability is abundant, aim is not.
What you point the tools at matters more than which tool you pick.
q: What is Thriving pointing AI tools at this week — and is that the highest-leverage target?

title: Before I Love Lucy, CBS Didn't Think America Would Accept Lucy's Real Husband
author: History Truth
ideas: Lucille Ball made CBS cast her real husband Desi Arnaz by proving the act on the road when the network said America wouldn't buy a Cuban bandleader as her TV spouse.
They took a pay cut to shoot on 35mm with three cameras and a live audience so they could stay in California—and Desilu kept ownership of the films.
That ownership deal and the three-camera sitcom grammar outlasted the ratings win.
q: What unfashionable casting or format fight would you take a pay cut for if it meant owning the episodes?

title: Reverse Engineer Anything (REA): 5 Places to Point Your AI
author: Nate B. Jones
ideas: REA lets Claude Code or Codex inspect real apps—even closed ones—and explain how a feature actually works.
Vibe-coded apps often look fine until you use them; reverse-engineering a working product turns fuzzy demos into specs you can rebuild.
Ask one finishable question (one behavior + the decision it informs), confirm the tools loaded with a tiny inspection, then turn a business rule into a checkable spec.
q: Which competitor microdrama format or internal Thriving tool would you reverse-engineer first so the next Claude-built pipeline doesn't collapse on first real use?

title: The AI CEO Dashboard Kit: An Excel Model, 14 Checks and 10 Claude Prompts
author: The AI Corner
ideas: Most founders know MRR; fewer can answer NRR or burn multiple without three exports and fragile formulas.
Paste a Stripe/CRM CSV into one workbook for 8 board KPIs, 4 charts, and 14 checks that catch bad data before a data room does.
The sample shows healthy growth with weak NRR—the number a pitch deck omits and diligence finds.
q: If you pasted PocketFM/StoryTV/Thriving revenue into this kit tomorrow, which of the 8 KPIs would scare you most—and which Claude prompt would you run first?

title: How to Design for Failures
author: ByteByteGo
ideas: You cannot build a failure-proof system; even perfect code depends on power, disks, and networks that fail.
Design for failure means deciding in advance how the system behaves when parts break—assume everything breaks.
Cover fault avoidance vs tolerance, blast-radius limits, correct operation during failure, and how you measure recovery.
q: When a generation model, queue, or editor step dies mid-episode, what should Thriving's pipeline do instead of hanging—and have you written that down?

title: The SwitchScreen: Vivian Yin's Vision for Premium Microdrama
author: ScreenMDM
ideas: Vertical is a new cinematic language, not a downgrade of cinema; the question is intention and craft, not duration.
The junk-food wave chased distribution and dopamine; the second wave must build IP longevity and believers, not buy users forever.
Taste cannot be taught like tools; design stories that can travel across formats (bigger screen, interactive, immersive).
q: Is Thriving optimizing for breakouts and IP that people share, or for disposable volume—and what would 'build believers, don't buy users' change in your next series greenlight?

title: Beat Sheet for a Vertical Micro-Drama
author: Versely Team
ideas: A 60–90s episode is not a compressed three-act film: use four beats—Resolve, Establish, Escalate, Cliff—~15–20s each.
Open mid-consequence from the last cliffhanger (no 'previously on'); cut before the new consequence lands so viewers return.
Write beat 4 first, lock one canonical character reference for the whole series, and treat release cadence as part of the craft.
q: Take your next episode script and force it into Resolve / Establish / Escalate / Cliff—which beat is soft, and did you write the cliffhanger before the middle?

title: Haiku 5.5 helper skill + CLAUDE.md note (comment LIMIT)
author: Instagram (storieswithpratik save)
ideas: A shareable Claude skill pairing a Haiku helper with a CLAUDE.md note.
Aimed at working around usage limits without abandoning the workflow.
Setup tips travel as comment-gated skills in the Claude creator community.
q: Would a Haiku helper + CLAUDE.md pattern help your studio stay productive when Claude rate-limits hit mid-pipeline?

title: Higgsfield Hit $1B in Annualized Revenue in 18 Months. Here Are Alex Mashrabov's 10 Calls
author: The AI Corner
ideas: Mashrabov burned more than $10M of a $16M seed chasing hype; with under $5M left he called customers, and eight creative directors all named the same gap: AI had no camera control, which decides whether a video can tell a story.

One customer went from a $99/month plan to a $6M/year deal in six months; the two buyers driving that spend are DTC brands testing hundreds of ads a week and short-form drama studios making whole shows with AI.

Treat video models as a rendering engine, not a benchmark: their open-sourced film averaged 3,000+ word prompts with 10+ image references per scene, and margins are 80%+ on open models versus 20-30% on closed ones.
q: Higgsfield names AI short-drama studios as one of its biggest buyers. If you called eight of your own directors and editors this week, what single missing control would they all name, and could Thriving own that answer?

title: What on earth is going on with AI pricing and packaging?
author: Elena Verna
ideas: Lovable's head of growth tears down AI pricing pages: plans promise '4x' or '15x more usage' of an amount they never state, or 500 million tokens a week with no idea what a token buys.
Unlike seat-based SaaS, AI companies are pricing work that neither the customer nor the company can predict, so credits and mystery limits have become the default.
Early adopters forgive it because the products are that good; she doubts the mass market will, and wants pricing tied to outcomes instead.
q: When a client buys a minute of Thriving output, do they know exactly what they're getting? How would you price by outcome (episodes delivered, retention hit) instead of by minute?

title: The President Was in His Pajamas When the Cuban Missile Crisis Began
author: History Truth
ideas: October 16, 1962: McGeorge Bundy had the U-2 photos of Soviet missile sites the night before and chose to let Kennedy sleep, then knocked on his bedroom door at 8:45 a.m.
Kennedy kept his schedule, quietly gathered a small group, and for six days the public knew nothing; a cut-short trip was explained as 'a cold'.
The 'also on this day' items include Walt Disney signing the 1923 Alice Comedies contract, nearly broke, after his first studio went bankrupt.
q: The whole thirteen-day crisis opens on one small, human beat: a knock on a bedroom door. What's the 'pajamas' detail that could open your next episode instead of the big event?

title: This Week in Charts: Agents Denied
author: a16z
ideas: Cloudflare data shows 403 'Forbidden' responses to bots and agents have roughly doubled since summer as big retailers like Amazon block agent shoppers.
Retailers fear losing customer relationships and ad eyeballs, plus fraud and returns, which have already roughly doubled and tripled since 2019.
Consumers use AI mostly for the middle of the journey (researching things they already found); 42% say they wouldn't trust AI to buy for them at all.
q: If audiences use AI to research but still want to make the final choice themselves, where in a viewer's path to your microdramas should AI help, and where should a human (or a cliffhanger) close the deal?

title: Is Anyone Watching Quibi?
author: Benjamin Wallace (Vulture)
ideas: Katzenberg raised $1.75B to sell 'quick bites' of Hollywood-quality video for the phone, signing Raimi, Elba, Teigen and others; the product (including Turnstyle vertical/horizontal viewing) was beautifully made.
It blocked screenshots to stay 'brand-safe', killing the social sharing a phone-native audience runs on, and its one quasi-viral moment (The Golden Arm) spread as camp, not as a hit.
Most subscribers came in on a 90-day free trial during a pandemic that erased the on-the-go viewing it was built for, so the real test was who would pay once it ended.
q: Quibi had premium short-form and big money but no shareability or habit; today's microdrama apps won with cheaper shows and relentless cliffhangers. Which Quibi mistake is Thriving closest to repeating, and which is it already past?

title: How Pixar Fosters Collective Creativity
author: Ed Catmull (Harvard Business Review)
ideas: Catmull opens by disagreeing with a studio head who said his problem was finding good ideas, not good people; Pixar's bet is that a great team will fix or replace a mediocre idea, while a mediocre team will ruin a great one.

Toy Story 2 was judged not good enough late in production and rebuilt with about nine months left, which became the lesson that quality has to be owned by the whole studio, not protected by a schedule.
The Braintrust gives directors blunt notes from peers but has no authority to force changes, and daily reviews of unfinished work make showing rough cuts normal instead of embarrassing.
q: At Thriving, who is your Braintrust, and does anyone see an episode while it's still rough enough to change cheaply?

title: Inside the black box of AI: How AI models actually think | Emmanuel Ameisen (Anthropic)
author: Lenny's Podcast
ideas: Anthropic interpretability researcher Emmanuel Ameisen argues the 'next-token predictor' framing undersells models: they form general representations of concepts and plan many tokens ahead without saying so.
Models are 'grown, not built', which is why looking inside them is closer to biology than reading code, and why some anthropomorphizing can be the right mental model.
What look like sudden capability jumps sit on smooth scaling curves underneath, and interpretability is how you check alignment instead of trusting outputs.
q: If a model really plans several beats ahead, how would you prompt or structure your AI writing pipeline to make it plan a whole episode's cliffhanger, not just the next line?

title: Notes on building things for people
author: Sari Azout (Sublime)
ideas: It's easy to measure what people do with your product and much harder to measure what it does to them; proxy metrics like clicks and time spent quietly distort incentives.
Azout calls out the 'wait-for-it' Reels genre that delays the point to farm watch time, and argues for values clear enough to work as a decision filter (no streaks at Sublime).
'How many people you touch beats how many people you reach': a small audience that loves you can matter more than a big one that barely notices.
q: Microdramas are built on cliffhangers that drive watch time. Where is the line for Thriving between a hook that earns the next episode and one that just farms it?

title: Why India Lacks An Nvidia
author: Govindraj Ethiraj (The Core)
ideas: Urban Company began when Abhiraj Singh Bhal couldn't get a carpenter to show up to hang paintings; the story repeats at Ixigo and Meesho, which now handles roughly 40% of India's e-commerce shipments.
Ethiraj's argument is that India's IIT-trained founders gravitate to the most glaring everyday breakdowns, so their brainpower goes to compensating for broken services rather than frontier tech.
He frames it as a lack of mindspace, not money: fix daily friction and infrastructure, and ambition rises toward world-beating products, rather than the state playing venture capitalist.
q: Thriving is an India-based team selling AI films to global buyers. Which everyday friction are you solving, and is it holding you back from the bigger bet?

title: Storyboard AI reels frame by frame before you generate anything
author: @thepiyushkukreja (storieswithpratik save)
ideas: Pick one visual style and stick to it so every frame looks like the same reel.
Write the script first, then storyboard it frame by frame before generating any shots.
Record the voiceover once for the whole piece instead of patching lines shot by shot.
q: Would a locked style and a frame-by-frame storyboard speed up your Almanac motion graphics and Thriving's AI episodes, or does it kill the happy accidents?

title: AI is ushering in an age of personal media
author: Benj Edwards (Understanding AI)
ideas: When the "band" costs nothing you no longer need the crowd: Suno turned his voice-memo song scraps into hundreds of tracks for an audience of one
A lot of personal media is nostalgia with a build system: people vibe-code remakes of games they loved as kids
He predicted on-demand AI movies in 2012 and now thinks he got the capability right but the economics wrong, since people may still want mass media as a shared cultural event
q: If anyone can prompt their own custom drama, what makes a Thriving show something people still want to watch together and talk about?

title: “Claude cuts my TikTok”: How this creator is scaling video with AI | Brooke Lacey
author: Claire Vo (How I AI, Lenny's Podcast Network)
ideas: Claude Code orchestrates FFmpeg, Whisper and Python so a raw phone take becomes a captioned vertical short in about 15 seconds; the whole edit lives in a TSV of start, end, shot size and label
She taught Claude her comedic timing (the pause before a punchline, which take had the best rhythm) through deliberate iteration, and she could only do that because she already knew the craft
Each video gets paired with its comments, and Claude pulls out what viewers questioned or wanted next, so the comment section becomes the content brief
q: Could the @thealmanac.hq edit live in a text file the way Brooke's does, so that one take turns into 15, 30 and 60 second cuts automatically?

title: The tribe has spoken: How Drop Your Buffs manages a community thousands of chats deep
author: Bailey Dunn with Sean Ross (On Substack)
ideas: They made the chat an event: live East and West Coast watch parties during Survivor hit about 3,200 comments in an hour, and that kind of real-time reaction is gone from algorithmic feeds
The lore, memes and inside jokes start in the chat, so "if you're not in the chat, you're getting half the story"
Fans who flew in alone for the live show had already found each other in the chat and met up beforehand, and the community now runs itself to the point where steering it gets the hosts roasted
q: What would a live watch-party ritual look like for a Thriving microdrama drop, where fans make the lore together between episodes?

title: Inside the World-Conquering Rise of the Micro-Drama
author: Chang Che (The New Yorker)
ideas: On a set in China shooting "Silent Ex-Wife" for Western viewers, two hours of content gets cut into about 60 episodes from a week of filming, on $100k to $300k budgets, often at the expense of labor standards

Analytics drive what gets greenlit. If a title doesn't take off on release day the algorithm drops it, so producers say "it's the audience and us co-deciding". ReelShort remakes proven arcs across sports and languages
The form serves a mostly female audience hungry for romance and underserved by Hollywood, and Chinese studios treat AI as routine ("We're basically an A.I. company now")
q: Where does Thriving sit between Shannon Yang's "a micro-drama is a product" and a story you'd actually call art?

title: I hacked my Kindle with Claude: no jailbreak, zero code
author: @sneha_sidequest
ideas: She plugged her Kindle into a laptop over USB and let Claude handle the rest.
All 470 of Lenny's newsletter posts became Kindle books.
The NYT and Times of India also land on the Kindle automatically.
q: Which of your newsletters would you actually read more if they showed up on a Kindle?

title: Model Behavior: Rick Rubin
author: Rick Rubin and Chris Best (On Substack)
ideas: Rubin treats AI like fire or any new instrument: early on you'll make bad sounds, then someone figures out how to play it well, so banning it too early throws the baby out with the bathwater.

He likes artists for their point of view, not their sound, and AI has no point of view to show you; Motown and K-pop already show a 'factory' world of popular music living next to the artist-driven one.
The wah-wah pedal story: Love's guitarist Johnny Echols threw the pedal in the trash, while Little Richard's driver Jimmy James kept it and became Jimi Hendrix.
q: Is AI your wah-wah pedal or your trombone imitation? What point of view does a Thriving film carry that a generic prompt never could?

title: Working Through Fear: An Interview with Blumhouse's Jason Blum
author: Scott Macaulay (Filmmaker Magazine)
ideas: Blumhouse's model joins independent production with studio distribution: budgets capped around $5M (Insidious cost $1M), set by what a film can earn back even if it never goes wide.

Directors get final cut and full creative control in exchange for no upfront money and a fixed budget. Blum hires experienced directors who 'know exactly what 21 days means', and final cut blew up on him only twice in 80 films.
'The scares are easy.' Every film needs an indie drama under the genre skin (The Purge is about gun control, Get Out about race), and test screenings decide which films get a wide release.
q: If you stripped the hooks and cliffhangers out of your next microdrama, is there still a story that holds up? And what's Thriving's version of the $5M ceiling and the deal with directors?

title: Dean Koontz: This is What Mystical Writing Feels Like
author: David Perell (How I Write)
ideas: Koontz stopped outlining so his characters could have 'free will', and went from an okay seller to a bestseller. If he isn't laughing or crying at his own pages, he backtracks to find where it went wrong.
The best plot twists are ones the writer doesn't see coming either. He polishes every page three times and writes about 10 hours a day, from 6 AM to 4 PM.
He won't use AI: you can't copyright what it writes, and it produces pastiche built from other people's books. To him, suspense is central to life itself, and it doesn't need horror or gore.
q: Koontz throws the outline away. Your AI pipeline needs a locked script. Where in Thriving's process can a character still surprise you?

title: We were spending $2,000 a day on generations until we figured out this one trick
author: PJ Ace (@PJaccetturo)
ideas: Genre.ai burned about $2,000 a day on Seedance generations for weeks making an episode of Nexus, until they locked shots before generating anything.

Claude runs Blender to block out compositions and cameras; those frames go in as storyboard references, plus character sheets with faces blanked except in the close-up profile shot. They share a Blender setup guide, and a BTS video shows the Dreamina process.
In replies: they keep episodes under 4 minutes for retention, and Seedance audio still has an 'echo' that's too expensive to fix with sound design from scratch.
q: What does a wasted generation cost Thriving per finished minute, and could a Claude-plus-Blender previz step pay for itself on the next episode?

title: Appeasement, Ohio
author: George Saunders (The New Yorker)
ideas: A new short story, free to read: Leo visits his Ohio cousin Maribeth for an eye-tissue donation from her son Kip, a big man who is now, along with his friend Mick, a Civil War denier.
Saunders got the idea from Helen Keller deniers: a country where everyone gets to be king of their own curated information, so doubting everything starts to feel like power.
The heart of the story is people tiptoeing around an obviously stupid idea for their own reasons (Leo needs the graft) and then finding out that avoiding it has consequences.
q: Saunders turns a family breakfast into satire about the whole country. What small domestic scene could carry a big idea in a Thriving episode?

title: Drama Queen
author: Meenal Baghel (The Big Indian Picture)
ideas: Ekta Kapoor's first pilot, Jeans 'n' Josh, was a dark show about peer pressure and AIDS. Star TV told her to bring something happy and family oriented. She took the note, and the happy family soaps that followed went on to define Indian television.

'It's not amazing talent that makes me special, but the sheer volume of work I have done.' Balaji ran about ten serials at once and made over seventy shows in fourteen years. She made a 21-year-old her creative head after he said his mother wouldn't buy a lead character's logic.

After a decade-long exclusive partnership, Star ended the deal, axed three soaps and sold its 26% stake, and the stock went into a tailspin. An insider explains the family system: Shobha plays hardball with channels by morning, and Jeetendra soothes the same executives over drinks by evening.
q: Kapoor built for 'women like his mother' and nearly went under when one buyer walked away. Who is Thriving's mother-in-the-audience, and what happens to the studio if PocketFM leaves?

title: He Deleted $7M in Revenue. Now His AI Data Company Is Worth $4B
author: Ari Dutilh (Solo Founders)
ideas: About three years ago one big customer, a future competitor, walked away and micro1 lost 60% of its revenue overnight. Instead of retreating, Ali Ansari went all in on that same market, and this month micro1 passed a $1B run rate, profitable, with about 180 people.

'Only the founding team can inject risk into the company.' He shut down a $7M-run-rate recruiting business with one Loom video, and later cancelled every human screening call in a single week. A few people nearly quit, and then the expert pool grew in step with revenue.

The async rules: whoever opens a thread proposes the fix and owns the final actions, people who add nothing stay out, and nobody says 'let's circle back next week'. In his model, progress is the quality of actions times the volume of actions.
q: micro1 nearly died when one account left. What is the one risky decision only you can make this quarter so that Thriving stops depending on a single client?

title: Why Doesn't Ancient Fiction Talk About Feelings?
author: Julie Sedivy (Nautilus, via Matter)
ideas: A saga from around 1230 has King Harold raise a fleet, win battles and rule Norway in three paragraphs without one line on how he felt. David Foster Wallace takes 12 pages to get a 13-year-old off a diving board, and all of it happens inside his head.

Medieval writers showed emotion through stock gestures like wringing hands and tearing hair. Between 1500 and 1700, characters started pausing mid-action for monologues about mixed desires, and the novel later added narrators who could see motives the characters couldn't.

Studies suggest heavy fiction readers are better at reading emotions from photos of eyes. Formulaic genre stories rely on stock characters with obvious motives, while literary fiction makes readers work out minds that surprise them.
q: Microdramas are closer to sagas: fast action, stock villains, emotions you can predict. Where could one surprising inner moment make a Thriving character feel real without slowing the episode?

title: Sume API: AI video models with 0% markup
author: David Im (@davidim)
ideas: His count of what resellers add on top of model prices: Higgsfield's API about 40% even at its best discount, Fal 100%, and Runway 414% on Seedance 2 480p.

Sume claims to pass the model cost straight through. Seedance 2.5 at 1080p is about 50% cheaper than Fal and Higgsfield and about 28% cheaper than Kie AI, pay as you go with no subscription, with a Higgsfield-style UI and an MCP/CLI for Claude.
His thesis: routing is never the moat. Model access will be a commodity, and the moats will be built at the application layer. The post drew about 800K views and 7K bookmarks.
q: If generation is about to get 30 to 50% cheaper, does Thriving keep the margin or pass it to PocketFM, and what in the studio is still hard to copy once anyone can buy the same models at cost?

title: An 86-minute guide to finding PMF | Rob Snyder (Author, The Power of Pull)
author: Lenny Rachitsky (Lenny's Podcast)
ideas: Snyder spent two years pushing a product the market didn't want before he stumbled onto what works. He has since helped more than 50 startups get from zero to $1M ARR.

PULL is the state of having demand: a Project on the buyer's to-do list that is Unavoidable right now, where the options they Look into are Lacking for a critical reason. When all four hold, customers pull the product out of your hands.

The episode covers where the best ideas come from, cold outreach and first sales calls, why he advises against design partners, and 'goblin mode' for when nothing is working. The full episode is free on YouTube, Spotify and Apple; Lenny's written takeaways are for paid subscribers.
q: Run Thriving's white-label agency pitch through PULL. Which agency owner has an unavoidable project this month, and why can't their current options deliver it?

title: How Squid Game Turned Rage and Desperation Into a Radical Hit
author: R.O. Kwon (Vanity Fair)
ideas: In 2009 Hwang Dong-hyuk, in debt along with his mother and grandmother, wrote Squid Game as a film. Investors called it too unrealistic and too violent, so it sat in a drawer for ten years.
By 2018 rising inequality made the premise feel real, and Netflix, newly building in Asia, turned it into a nine-episode series. Within ten days it was the most watched Netflix show in 90 countries.

Hwang built it on gambling because desperate people drop their masks and show 'very pure emotions'. He kept rewriting scenes the night before shooting, such as the dying Sang-woo reaching out a hand to Gi-hun, to find a glimpse of humanity in a villain.
q: Which of Thriving's shelved or rejected story ideas might the moment have caught up with, and what is the one raw emotion your next series is built on?

title: Databricks & the Future of the Firm
author: a16z
ideas: Databricks has passed a $7 billion revenue run rate, growing 80% a year. It now sees more queries from agents than from people, and agents launch more than 17 million databases on it every day.

The piece argues agents need a shared system of record (what is true, what data means, who can do what, what worked) so people and agents can act without routing every decision through layers of managers.
The long-run change isn't 'everyone is an engineer' but 'everyone is a manager': agents handle work that's already figured out, and people judge what's good and decide what should exist next.
q: If your agents and editors all worked from one shared record of what each client wants and what passed QC, which decisions could stop waiting on you?

title: Let Chaos Reign, and Then Rein In Chaos
author: a16z (Replit essay)
ideas: Written for the launch of Replit for Business: most AI agents today live in chaos, in chat windows, personal accounts and one-off scripts, and nobody can see what they did.

PCs, spreadsheets and email all entered offices the same messy way, with people lying on purchase forms to get PCs and 'rogue spreadsheets' that only their maker understood. The winners built a habitat instead of a ban.
The goal is 'free-range' agents: not caged, not running wild, but inside rules for access, audit and versioning that keep the bottom-up energy alive.
q: Which of your team's personal AI hacks should become a shared, logged studio workflow, and which should stay free-range?

title: Give Claude 17M+ free films and 14M audio recordings for video edits
author: @ElliotPadfield
ideas: The Internet Archive has a free API that needs no key, documented at archive.org/developers.
It holds 10,000+ public-domain Prelinger films for stock and archival b-roll, 187,000 78rpm records and 300,000+ live concert recordings.
His suggested standing instruction to Claude: whenever you need archival b-roll or period music, search the Prelinger and 78rpm collections and use them in the edit.
q: Could Almanac reels or period microdramas pull free archival b-roll and music instead of generating every shot, and what licence check would you need first?
